title: Human-Centered Corrective Control in Semi-Automatic Construction Machinery: Enhancing Stability and Operator Intent Integration
content: Semi-automatic piloting combines automated motion reproduction with operator corrections, but the stability of iterative correction remains unclear. We investigated whether corrective lever inputs converge across repeated interactions and how task complexity, baseline-trajectory source, and feedback-reflection condition affect this behavior. Two skilled excavator operators with contrasting operating tendencies were selected to explore individual differences and examine within-operator reproducibility across repeated correction cycles. They used a simulator to correct prerecorded grading and loading actions under Self-Correction and Other-Correction conditions, with corrections either immediately reflected (Apply) or recorded without immediate reflection (No Apply). Stability was evaluated from changes in the root mean square (RMS) magnitude of corrective lever inputs across correction cycles and explored using generalized estimating equations. Corrective lever inputs generally converged during grading in the Apply condition. During loading, corrective lever inputs tended to diverge, particularly for the Swing axis, and immediate reflection did not consistently restore convergence. Whether operators corrected their own or another operator’s baseline trajectory had less influence than task and feedback-reflection condition. These results suggest that visual feedback alone may be insufficient to support stable corrections in complex multi-axis tasks. Because the study involved two operators, a simulator, a fixed task order, and an input-level proxy rather than direct excavation performance, the findings are exploratory. Larger studies should test whether feedback and adaptive assistance improve corrective-input stability and task outcomes.
